name: Iris Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hello! Yes, of course. I like talking about this, so you may get long answers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying computer science, so I'm on campus Monday to Thursday and I commute from the village where I grew up, about half an hour by train. I live at home with my parents, Greta and Klaus, and my grandfather Otto. Friday and Saturday evenings I work in the kitchen at Luigi's pizzeria, and on Sundays after church I sell handmade candles at the village market. I use an AI assistant every day for coding help, planning and drafting emails for my candle orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected, and I'm quite relaxed about it. I'd tell people it helps with small things, like my candle shop descriptions, but it doesn't change life. At Luigi's my boss Enzo would laugh and say pizza dough doesn't care about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan goes on as it is. I'd finish the degree and look for a good job within an hour of home. I want to stay near my family, because my grandfather Otto isn't well. The pressure is money: I have almost no savings, and my parents can't give me anything extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Luigi's and keep growing the candle stall, aiming to sell online as well. I'd use the AI to write product pages and plan my stock. And I'd save a fixed amount each month, because I want to be able to help with Otto's care costs when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. There's a low hum of money worry, but I'm used to it, and I like being busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Otto's care costs. What do you expect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's eighty-one and had a fall last winter. My parents pay for a carer two mornings a week, and it's a stretch. I'd like to be earning enough that nobody has to choose between a carer and the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the candle business going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small but steady. I make about forty a weekend in profit, and I've got a few regulars from church. Each sale feels like proof that I can build something, even if it's tiny.

say: I'd say it's what I expected, and it helps with **small things** like product descriptions.
I'd quote Enzo: pizza dough doesn't care about AI.
think: My plan goes on: finish the degree and find a good job within an hour of **home**.
Money is the pressure, with almost no savings and **Otto's care** ahead.
do: Keep working at Luigi's and grow the **candle stall** online.
Use AI to write product pages and plan stock.
Save a fixed amount each month for family **care costs**.
feel: **Good**, mostly, with a low hum of money worry.
S0.quote: I'd like to be earning enough that nobody has to choose between a carer and the electricity bill.
fieldNote: Ordinary stress is **family care**: her grandfather's fall and her parents' stretched finances.
Uses AI daily for the **candle business**, so a plateau barely touches her.
Wants to stay near home, a traditional, community-minded plan.

steps.text: Keep the Friday and Saturday shifts at Luigi's pizzeria
Start an online candle shop beside the village stall
Save a fixed amount monthly for Otto's care costs
Use AI to write product pages and plan candle stock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I'd call real change, and the right response is to work, not to complain. I'd tell people in the village that AI can help small businesses like the bakery and the farm shop, if somebody shows them how. I'd say it at church too, because people there worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm well placed. I use these tools every day, and my degree is the kind that lets me build them into things. The jobs that get squeezed are the junior coding jobs in big firms, and I'd rather work for a small local company or start one. I think there's a gap in helping small businesses in places like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start offering a small service to local businesses, like setting up online ordering for the farm shop. I'd build it in my spare time with AI tools, and charge a fair price. I'd go to the next chamber of commerce meeting and introduce myself. And I'd still work at Luigi's, since I like the steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the change in the economy overall, but I feel I can do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people at church worry. What do they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Brandt, who runs the church office, asked me if her job would disappear. I told her it would change, and I offered to show her how to use a tool for the newsletter. She laughed and said she was too old, but she came the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think everyone can adapt like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly no. I've got a head start because I'm young and I like gadgets. I think people should be helped by their communities and employers to learn, not left alone. I'd be happy to help, but I can't do it for everyone.

say: I'd say it's **real change** and the right response is to work, not complain.
I'd tell the village AI can help small businesses like the **farm shop**.
think: I'm well placed, since I use these tools **daily** and can build them into things.
Junior coding jobs in big firms get squeezed, so I'd rather work **locally**.
do: Offer **online ordering** setup to local businesses like the farm shop.
Introduce myself at the next chamber of commerce meeting.
Keep working at Luigi's for steady money.
feel: **Excited**, a bit nervous about the wider economy.
S1.quote: The jobs that get squeezed are the junior coding jobs in big firms, and I'd rather work for a small local company or start one.
fieldNote: Sees a **gap** in helping small businesses in places like hers, a free-market, community-minded view.
Helps older neighbours kindly, like Mrs Brandt at the church office, and admits she cannot help **everyone**.
Fully adaptive: builds, charges a fair price and networks.

steps.text: Set up online ordering for the farm shop as my first client
Build a reusable ordering template with AI tools
Keep the Luigi's pizzeria shifts for steady money
Introduce myself at the next chamber of commerce meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and it's happening far too quickly for families and small towns. I'd say we should look after our neighbours, and I'd suggest the church group organise help for people who lose work. I'd also say governments should not ban it, because that wouldn't work, but they should protect people who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the whole structure of work is shaken. By 2029 I'd be graduating into nothing, and by 2031 the hands-on jobs where my parents work would go too. My father fixes farm machinery and my mother cooks in a school, so they'd have a few more years, but not many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree because I'd need every skill I can get, and I'd go hard on the AI side. I'd grow the candle business and the small-business service quickly, since they don't depend on a big employer. I'd talk to my parents about their savings and about who in the village might help with Otto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and honestly sad. I'd feel like the village I love is going to change faster than anyone is ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to your parents the night you decided to go all in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, Mum, I'm going to do the business seriously now, and I'd like us to make a plan for money. I'd ask them to show me their savings, which they'd hate. But I think we'd be better off knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said governments shouldn't ban it. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a ban would only push it elsewhere and leave us behind. I believe in letting people build and trade, but with a safety net for those who can't keep up. It's a balance, and nobody has proved how to get it right.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and happening much too fast for families and small towns.
I'd suggest the church group help neighbours who lose work, and governments protect people rather than **ban** AI.
think: The whole structure of **work** is shaken, and I'd graduate into nothing by 2029.
My parents' hands-on jobs get a few extra years, but not many.
do: Stay in the degree and go hard on the **AI side**.
Grow the candle shop and small-business service fast.
Ask my parents to show me their **savings** and make a plan.
feel: **Alarmed** and sad, because the village I love will change faster than anyone is ready for.
S2.quote: I believe in letting people build and trade, but with a safety net for those who can't keep up.
fieldNote: Her **free-market** instinct holds even under pressure, paired with community safety nets.
Her business ideas become the main plan because they don't depend on a big **employer**.
Sadness about the **village** shows how rooted she is.

steps.text: Grow the candle shop and the small-business service this term
Go deeper on AI coding tools for client projects
Sit down with my parents to go through their savings
Ask the church group to organise help for people losing work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is a useful gap, and that we should use it to build things in our community. I'd say the village needs a few people who can show the others how to use the tools. I'd offer to do that myself at the library on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to graduate in 2029, build a business and be comfortably settled before the big change lands. The hands-on jobs around me, like my dad's repair work, would last until about 2034. That gives my family a few more years of normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small company during my degree, doing online ordering and simple software for small businesses. I'd hire someone local part-time as soon as I could afford it. I'd also keep my savings in something safe, and I'd probably buy a small second-hand van for deliveries, if the money allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. It feels like a good time to be young and willing to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire someone local. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a village stays alive when people have work they can do near home. I don't want to build something that makes people leave. I'd like to be an employer who knows everyone's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clients could ask the AI directly and not need me, or a large firm could undercut me. I'd handle that by being the person who turns up and fixes things, which a chatbot can't do. Trust is a product too.

say: I'd say five years is a useful gap, and we should use it to **build** things in our community.
I'd offer to show neighbours how to use the tools at the library on **Saturdays**.
think: I'd have time to graduate and build a **business** before the big change lands.
My dad's repair work lasts until about **2034**, giving my family a few more normal years.
do: Start a small company during my degree, doing **online ordering** and simple software.
Hire someone local part-time when I can afford it.
feel: **Hopeful**; it feels like a good time to be young and willing to try things.
S3.quote: A village stays alive when people have work they can do near home.
fieldNote: Five years makes her a **builder**: a company, a local hire and Saturday help sessions.
Her business is also a community aim: keeping **work** in the village.
Aware that clients might use AI directly and plans to compete on trust.

steps.text: Register a small company for online ordering and simple software
Run a Saturday session at the library showing neighbours AI tools
Keep my savings in a safe account, not in shares
Plan with my parents how to keep Otto's carer going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great opportunity, and people should be excited as long as they're willing to work for it. I'd tell the village that there's time to learn, and the library could run classes. At church I'd say it's good to plan, but also to trust that there's a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can do the degree, get a few years of experience and start my business with some savings behind me. I'd probably be married or close to it, with a house nearby. I'd want my children to grow up in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work part-time for a local firm and slowly grow the business. I'd keep using AI tools daily, and I'd teach local people what I know. I'd also save towards a small house, because ten years is a good time to plan for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd still have days of nerves, but I'd feel I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned being married with children nearby. How does the change fit with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I can plan it in a normal order: degree, job, home, family. If it happened in two years, I'd have to put all that on hold, and that would make me sad. Ten years lets me keep the life I want: a degree, a job, a home and a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope the village looks like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same faces, a few more small businesses and a better internet connection. I'd like Otto's house to be a place where my children visit, even if Otto isn't here anymore.

say: I'd say ten years is a great **opportunity** as long as people are willing to work for it.
I'd suggest the library run **classes** so the village can learn.
think: I can do the degree, gain experience and start my **business** with some savings.
I'd want my **children** to grow up in the village.
do: Finish the degree and work part-time for a local firm.
Keep using AI daily and **teach** local people.
feel: **Calm**; I'd have nervous days, but I'd feel I can steer.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me keep the life I want: a degree, a job, a home and a family.
fieldNote: The one scenario where she feels **calm**, because her traditional life order stays intact.
Connects the AI future to a **village** with small firms and better internet.
Wants to teach others, which is a pattern across her answers.

steps.text: Work part-time for a local firm after the degree
Save towards a small house near the village
Grow the candle and software business slowly
Teach local people AI tools at the library

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is not enough time for the village, my grandfather's care or my own plans, and it breaks the order of life I want. What would help is a safety net for people who lose work, training that reaches small towns and not just cities, and small-business support so local firms can use these tools too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume adaptable means unbothered. I use the tools every day and I still feel the weight of my family's money. I'd like to say you can be both ready and worried.

headlineQuote: I use the tools every day and I still feel the weight of my family's money.
portrait: **Iris** is an eighteen-year-old computer science student who lives in her village, works in a pizza kitchen and sells handmade candles.
She uses **AI tools** daily, backs free markets with a community safety net, and wants to keep work local.
Her **family** shapes her answers: her grandfather's care costs, her parents' hands-on jobs and a wish to stay near home.
Two years leave her anxious; with ten she feels calm because her traditional order of life stays intact.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because two years breaks the village, her grandfather's care and the order of life she wants.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** for people who lose work, training that reaches small towns, and small-business support for local firms.
